name: Fatima Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Fatima. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a young firm that only does cloud accounting, mostly for startups and creative freelancers: illustrators, game studios, a couple of podcast companies. I spend the morning on month-end accounts and VAT returns, which is the sales tax businesses collect and pay over, and the afternoon building automations so bank feeds sort themselves. I love the building part. What wears me out is clients who send me a photo of a receipt at 11pm on a Sunday.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How much do you use AI tools now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day, for nearly everything. I've got a chat tool open all day to draft client emails, explain tax rules, and write little scripts that match invoices to payments. I still check every number before it leaves the building. My partner Theo says I talk to it more than I talk to him, which isn't far off during VAT week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a great tool that got sold as magic, and I'd keep using it every day. Online I'd probably post a thread about the boring wins: saved hours, fewer typos.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be fine, honestly. My job's safe, my automations keep working, and I'm the person colleagues come to when something breaks. The only worry is Theo's freelance sound work, which goes up and down whatever AI does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep building automations at work and ask for a pay review based on the hours they save. I'd keep about four months of savings, which covers us when Theo has a quiet month. Maybe I'd start a small newsletter on cloud accounting tips for freelancers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A little disappointed, actually, because I was excited for something bigger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask for a pay review based on hours saved. Would the firm agree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe half. The partners like the savings but they like keeping them too. I'd bring numbers. My bank-feed rules saved about six hours a week across the team last quarter, and I'd want some of that back in my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does Theo's work affect your money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some months he earns double what I do, and some months nothing. We split rent by what each of us made that month. I'm the steady one, which is funny, because I'm also the one who likes risk.

say: I'd call AI a **great tool** that got sold as magic.
I'd post about the **boring wins**: saved hours and fewer typos.
think: My job feels **safe**, and colleagues come to me when automations break.
The only real worry is **Theo's freelance** income going up and down.
do: Ask for a **pay review** based on the six hours a week saved.
Keep about **four months** of savings to cover Theo's quiet months.
Start a small **newsletter** with cloud accounting tips for freelancers.
feel: **Calm**, and a bit disappointed it wasn't bigger.
S0.quote: My bank-feed rules saved about six hours a week across the team last quarter, and I'd want some of that back in my pay.
fieldNote: Fatima sees AI as a **pay argument**: she wants a share of the savings.
Her steady salary anchors a household with **irregular freelance** income.
She is mildly **disappointed** that the big change didn't come.
A **side newsletter** hints at entrepreneurial instincts.

steps.text: Ask the partners for a pay review backed by hours saved
Keep building bank-feed automations for the client accounts
Launch a newsletter on cloud accounting tips for freelancers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is when we decide who gets the gains. At work I'd say let's cut hours, not people, and I'd post about a four-day week for accountants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd probably do well. I'm already the person building the tools, so I'd become more useful, not less. But I'd watch the firm stop hiring juniors, and that would bother me, because I came up through that exact junior role three years ago.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pitch an AI lead role to the partners within a month, with a pay rise attached. I'd keep the newsletter going and maybe charge for a short course. I'd also push the firm to keep taking one junior a year, even if their work looks different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly excited, with a sour bit about the juniors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Liam, our junior, who's 22 and still learning to read a balance sheet. Last year his job was mostly bank coding, and that's gone in this picture. I'd want to make sure he's learning the judgement parts, not just clicking approve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You want hours cut, not people. Would you take fewer hours yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if the pay held. A four-day week would let me do the course and spend time with Theo. A four-day week with the same pay is fair, but fewer hours with less pay is just a pay cut with a nice name.

say: I'd say we must decide **who gets the gains** from AI.
I'd push for a **four-day week**: cut hours, not people.
think: I'd likely **do well**, since I already build the tools.
It would bother me to see the firm **stop hiring juniors**.
do: Pitch an **AI lead role** with a pay rise within a month.
Turn the newsletter into a **paid short course**.
Push to keep hiring **one junior a year**.
feel: Mostly **excited**, with a **sour edge** about the juniors.
S1.quote: A four-day week with the same pay is fair, but fewer hours with less pay is just a pay cut with a nice name.
fieldNote: Fatima expects to **gain** in this picture and says so honestly.
Her politics show in the **four-day week** and junior hiring push.
She worries for **Liam**, seeing herself three years ago.
Draws a sharp line between **fewer hours** and a disguised pay cut.

steps.text: Pitch an AI lead role with a pay rise to the partners
Turn the newsletter into a paid short course for freelancers
Push the firm to keep hiring one junior accountant a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments should tax the companies selling AGI and pay people through the change. At work I'd say we need to be honest with clients and each other, not pretend it's business as usual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my edge disappears. Building automations was my thing, and AGI builds them better. Accounting is all thinking work, so there's no three-year cushion for me. And Theo's sound work could get hit by AI music tools too, so both incomes wobble at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast. In the first few months I'd use the tools to set up my own one-person practice for creative freelancers, charging less than the firm, while there's still a window. I'd get our savings past six months and cancel the trip to Lisbon. And I'd join whatever group is pushing for an AI tax, because this can't land only on workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly. Even someone who usually likes change gets scared when the deadline is two years away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why start your own practice if AGI can do the work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a year or two, clients will still want a person they trust to sign off, so I'd sell that trust while it still means something. After that, I don't know, maybe I'd be helping people understand their own money rather than doing their books.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said both incomes wobble at once. What happens at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd sit down with a spreadsheet, of course. Theo would take any steady work he can, like live sound at venues, because that's hands-on and robots come later. I'd cover rent while he does that.

say: I'd call for an **AI tax** to pay people through the change.
I'd urge **honesty with clients** instead of business as usual.
think: My **automation edge** vanishes, since AGI builds them better.
Both **our incomes wobble** at once, with no hands-on cushion for me.
do: Set up a **one-person practice** for freelancers within months.
Push savings past **six months** and cancel the **Lisbon trip**.
Join a group pushing for an **AI tax**.
feel: The **speed** is what frightens me most.
S2.quote: For a year or two, clients will still want a person they trust to sign off, so I'd sell that trust while it still means something.
fieldNote: Even the **most adaptive** person here is alarmed by speed.
Her plan is a **short window**: sell trust before it loses value.
Theo's shift to **live sound** uses the robot delay well.
She blames **AI sellers**, wanting them taxed, not workers.

steps.text: Set up a one-person practice for freelancers within months
Push household savings past six months
Cancel the Lisbon trip and hold off on extras
Join a campaign pushing for a tax on AI companies

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to plan if firms and government start now. I'd be loud about it at work and online, and push for retraining funds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could ride it for a while. I'd have three or four good years being the AI person, building savings, before AGI arrives in 2031. After that I'd need a job with people at its centre, and I'd want to have started it already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the AI lead role and save hard, aiming for nine months of savings by 2029. I'd train part-time as a financial coach for freelancers, someone who helps people cope with irregular money, not just files it. And I'd talk to Theo about whether we buy a flat now or wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wired, a bit. Half excited, half worried, which is pretty much how I feel about most things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a flat now, or wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wait, I think. Buying a flat on two incomes that might both shrink by 2031 feels reckless. Theo wants to buy, because his parents never owned anything. That's a real argument we'd have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why financial coaching rather than something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because people with irregular income are scared of money, and talking them through it is the bit of my job people thank me for. Even with AGI, I think someone anxious wants a person across the table.

say: I'd say five years is enough to **plan** if we start now.
think: I'd have three or four **good years** as the AI person.
After 2031 I need work with **people at its centre**.
do: Take the **AI lead role** and save toward nine months.
Train part-time as a **financial coach** for freelancers.
Hold off **buying a flat** with Theo for now.
feel: **Half excited, half worried**, as with most changes.
S3.quote: Buying a flat on two incomes that might both shrink by 2031 feels reckless.
fieldNote: Five years gives Fatima a clear **two-stage plan**: ride, then pivot.
Her pivot is **financial coaching**, built on the part clients thank her for.
A real **disagreement with Theo** about buying a flat surfaced.
She still expects her **accounting role** to end.

steps.text: Take the AI lead role at the firm
Save toward nine months of household cover by 2029
Train part-time as a financial coach for freelancers
Delay buying a flat with Theo until after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this well, and that it's a political choice whether we do. I'd want a long-term plan for accountants: retraining, shorter hours, a share of the gains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd have a whole career arc before AGI lands. I'd be 37. I could run my own small firm with AI doing the books and me doing the advice. Then, close to 2036, I'd shift into coaching full time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the firm two years as the AI lead, then go independent. I'd invest some savings in the business: software, a website, a proper office share. I'd keep training as a coach slowly, a module a term.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, mostly. I'd feel like I was steering, not being dragged.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your own firm with AI doing the books. Isn't that the thing you'd campaign against?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha, yes, a bit. But I'd pay myself fairly and share the gains with anyone I hire. I'd rather be an example of running an AI firm decently than refuse and watch someone worse do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Theo say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Theo would say go for it, and then panic about the website costs. He'd probably do the sound for my coaching videos. That's how we work: I plan, he makes it sound good.

say: I'd say ten years lets us **do this well**, if politics chooses to.
I'd want a **long-term plan** for accountants.
think: I'd have a **whole career arc** before AGI lands.
I could run a **small firm** with AI doing the books.
do: Stay **two years** as AI lead, then go independent.
**Invest savings** in software, a website and an office share.
Keep training as a **coach**, one module a term.
feel: Mostly **good**, steering rather than being dragged.
S4.quote: I'd rather be an example of running an AI firm decently than refuse and watch someone worse do it.
fieldNote: Fatima admits the tension between her **politics** and her plans.
Ten years turns fear into a **business plan**.
Still, her **accounting work** ends by 2036, so some worry stays.
**Theo** is a creative partner, not just a second income.

steps.text: Invest savings in software, a website and an office share
Run a small firm where AI handles the bookkeeping
Take one financial coaching module each term
Leave the firm after two years to go independent

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's no time to sell trust or train for anything. What would help is a tax on AI companies that pays people while they retrain, and some support for freelancers like Theo who fall through every safety net.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the juniors much. If firms stop hiring them, there's no one to become a senior in ten years. That's a hole nobody's talking about.

headlineQuote: Even someone who usually likes change gets scared when the deadline is two years away.
portrait: Fatima is a **27-year-old** cloud accountant who uses AI tools **every day**.
She lives with Theo, a **freelance sound engineer**, and is the household's steady earner.
She wants AI gains **shared**, through taxes, fair pay and shorter weeks.
She feels fine in the slow pictures but **alarmed** by AGI in 2028.
Her long plan is **financial coaching**, built on the part clients thank her for.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, as there's no time to pivot or sell trust.
whatWouldHelp: A **tax on AI companies** funding retraining.
Support for **freelancers** who fall through safety nets.
